title: U.S. Just Had Its Hottest Summer in 132 Years, NOAA Reports
summary: If this summer felt unbearable, you're not alone — it was officially the hottest summer ever recorded in the United States in at least 132 years. According to a new report from NOAA (the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration), temperatures from June through August averaged 3 degrees Fahrenheit (1.67 degrees Celsius) above normal, beating the previous record set in 2021. August alone was the hottest August ever measured, at 3.5°F above average. But the heat was only part of the story. This summer was also the third driest on record for the contiguous U.S. (the adjoining states, excluding Alaska and Hawaii). By September 1, 59.1% of the country was in drought, with over 75% of Puerto Rico affected — 40% of it in "extreme drought." Dry conditions raised wildfire risk. In August, fires burned over 10,000 acres in eastern Washington and spread into Oregon. More fires broke out in Nevada and Alaska. Wind gusts up to 111 miles per hour (178.6 km/h) tore across South Dakota. A heatwave scorched south Florida, and Hurricane Lala brought intense winds, rain, and flooding to Hawaii. While a 3-degree difference might not sound like much, scientists say it has massive consequences. Climate change, driven primarily by greenhouse gas emissions from human activities like transportation and manufacturing, is making extreme weather more common. The drought is projected to continue in many areas, meaning the risk of wildfires and other disasters will likely worsen. As the planet warms, these record-breaking events are expected to become more frequent and more severe.
why_it_matters: Today's teenagers will live their adult lives inside the climate these records are measuring — the water rules, wildfire seasons, insurance costs, food prices, and school heat days of the next few decades are being decided now.

background_read: NOAA (the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) is the U.S. government agency that runs weather forecasts and keeps climate records stretching back to the 1800s, which is how it can rank one summer against more than a century of others.

Puerto Rico (a U.S. territory in the Caribbean) is not part of the contiguous U.S., but it was counted separately here, with more than three-quarters of the island in drought and a large share in 'extreme drought' — a reminder that drought hits islands and mainland regions very differently.

The United States has been through drought disasters before, most famously the Dust Bowl that struck the Great Plains in the 1930s, when dry soil blew away in huge storms and pushed thousands of farming families to leave their land.

Scientists use tools like the U.S. Drought Monitor, a weekly map that combines rainfall, soil moisture, and stream data, to decide which areas count as being in drought — the same measurements behind the 59.1% figure in the report.

The IPCC (the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, a United Nations body that summarizes climate research for governments) has long warned that heat waves, droughts, and heavy rains become more frequent and more severe as the planet warms, under international agreements such as the Paris Agreement.

perspectives.description: Better monitoring and forecasting, like NOAA's records and the U.S. Drought Monitor, let cities, farmers, and emergency crews prepare days ahead instead of reacting. Some regions with longer growing seasons may even gain from warmer temperatures in the short run, though those gains come with new risks.

The burden falls hardest on farmers, outdoor workers, low-income households without air conditioning, and places like Puerto Rico that are already strained. Continuing greenhouse gas emissions mean the underlying cause is not being addressed, and record-breaking heat and drought are treated as a pattern rather than a one-off.

Climate scientists distinguish between natural year-to-year variability and a long-term warming trend; single records matter less than the steady stacking of them. The summer's combination of extreme heat and extreme dryness fits exactly what models have projected for a warming planet, which is why agencies keep close records over more than a century.

The report projects continued drought in many areas, meaning more wildfire risk and tighter water supplies. The coming debates are about adaptation — fireproofing towns, changing crops, redesigning cities — and about how quickly emissions can be cut, since every fraction of a degree changes how often these records fall.
